subject: Climate & Environment
title: California's Fire Crisis
description: A short lesson to help you apply California's Fire Crisis.

hook.text: California's fire season used to last four months. Now it's nearly year-round.

buildup.text: Decades of fire suppression left forests overgrown. Dead wood accumulated as fuel.

discovery.text: Drought, heat waves, and Santa Ana winds create explosive conditions every autumn.

twist.text: The Camp Fire in 2018 destroyed the town of Paradise in hours, killing 85 people.

climax.text: Insurance companies are leaving California. Millions of homes are becoming uninsurable.

punchline.text: The state that symbolizes the future is already living the climate crisis.

quiz.question: Why did decades of fire suppression make California's fires worse?
options: Dead wood accumulated as fuel in overgrown forests

details.summary: California faces an escalating wildfire crisis driven by hotter, drier conditions, prolonged drought, decades of fire suppression that built up fuels, and expanding development into fire-prone wildlands. The state now experiences its largest fires in recorded history nearly every year.
details.whyItMatters: California's fire crisis previews what many regions face as climate change transforms fire regimes. Billions in damage and thousands of destroyed homes demand new approaches.
takeaways: Climate change has doubled fire-prone area in California since the 1970s
Over 20,000 structures were destroyed by wildfires between 2017 and 2021
Fire suppression created dense fuel loads that now burn catastrophically

faq.question: Why have California fires gotten so much worse?
faq.answer: Warming has dried vegetation earlier, extended fire seasons, and combined with a century of fire suppression that allowed fuel to accumulate. Simultaneously, millions of homes have been built in the wildland-urban interface where fire risk is highest.

faq.question: What is the wildland-urban interface?
faq.answer: The WUI is the zone where homes and wildland vegetation meet or intermingle. Fourteen million homes in the US are in the WUI, and this number grows each year as development pushes into forested hills and grasslands.
